newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls as U.S. trade gap expands.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls as U.S. trade gap expands.

text.p: NEW YORK, Sept 18 - The dollar fell against most leading currencies on Wednesday on news that the U.S. international trade deficit unexpectedly ballooned by 42.6 percent in July.

However, the U.S. currency trimmed its losses late in the day amid talk that the Bank of Japan might be considering intervening to support the dollar and as dealers judged the dollar's drop as too rapid.

The Commerce Department reported that the overall U.S. trade gap widened to $11.68 billion in July, the highest since the fourth quarter of 1987 when monthly deficits averaged $12.9 billion. In June, the trade shortfall stood at $8.19 billion.
The trade figures surprised currency traders because Wall Street economists had forecast an overall deficit of $8.8 billion in July. The announcement spurred a flood of dollar selling.

"If you run a trade deficit, that basically means that you're importing more goods than you're exporting. It's going to create more demand for foreign currency than it does for your own currency. Hence the dollar becomes devalued," said Bob Lynch, a senior currency analyst at MMS International.
Dollar declines accelerated after the currency fell below key technical levels around 110 Japanese yen and 1.5120 German marks as previously set sell orders were triggered.
In late trading, the dollar stood at 1.5090 marks, down from 1.5143 marks late Tuesday. The dollar fell to 109.12 yen from 110.35 yen.

The United States' politically sensitive trade shortfall with Japan jumped 32.9 percent to $4.31 billion in July from the previous month. Deterioration in that deficit prompted general demand for yen, and traders also sold some European currencies and purchased yen.
"The real selling today has been marks for yen," said William Marr, manager of foreign exchange at Credit Commerciale de France.

The bulk of the dollar's losses came shortly after the trade data were released. Later in the New York session, rumours swept through the market that the Bank of Japan was checking the dollar-yen exchange rate with an eye to possibly buying dollars and selling yen, traders said.
"That in addition to an oversold condition short term caused the dollar to back up a little bit off the lows," said Debra Doerr-Larsen, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Commerzbank.

The Bank of Japan's New York office declined to comment on the rumours. In the past, the Bank of Japan has intervened in the foreign exchange market to keep the dollar higher against the yen in an effort to help Japanese manufacturers competitiveness abroad.

France's conservative government presented on Wednesday a 1997 budget that aims to revive growth by cutting taxes while reducing the budget deficit to guarantee the country a place in European monetary union slated to begin in January 1999.
"Government officials had pretty much leaked a good portion of that out to the press already," said Lynch, adding the impact on the foreign exchange market was marginal.
In other trade, the British pound rose to $1.5615 on Wednesday from $1.5560 on Tuesday. The dollar fell to 1.2420 Swiss francs from 1.2445 francs but inched higher to Canadian $1.3718 from C$1.3712.
